title: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Spokane, WA: 6-Day Course
description: Six-day AWS CWI exam prep for Spokane aerospace, aluminum, structural steel and bridge inspectors: WABO examiner route, Part C choice, Part B travel.
h1: AWS CWI Exam Preparation in Spokane: Six Days for Inland Northwest Aerospace, Fabrication, Structural Steel and Bridge Inspectors
html:
Spokane is a manufacturing city that people on the coast tend to overlook. Aluminum plate for airliners comes off the rolls at Trentwood in Spokane Valley, aircraft component and finishing shops line the industrial parks along the Spokane River, KC-135 tankers fly from Fairchild Air Force Base west of town, and the North Spokane Corridor is adding miles of new freeway and bridges through the city. All of that keeps welders busy and keeps a steady demand for people who can inspect their work to a code. In Washington the AWS Certified Welding Inspector (CWI) credential also sits inside the state's structural welder certification system, which gives it a particular local value.

Atlantis NDT runs a six-day course that prepares Inland Northwest candidates for the CWI examination: welders and lead hands, fabrication and machine shop quality staff, aerospace supplier inspectors, NDT technicians and engineers. The American Welding Society sets the exam, runs it and certifies those who pass; candidates apply to AWS one by one and must each meet its eligibility and vision rules. AWS has not approved or endorsed the course, and Atlantis has no access to exam content. There is no Atlantis classroom in Spokane. An individual can work through the six days online at their own pace and send questions to an instructor, an employer can host the six days for a group at its own site, and a candidate who wants personal coaching can book one-to-one sessions, online or in person at a location agreed when booking. The day-by-day plan is on the AWS CWI exam prep page.

Aluminum plate, aircraft parts and an air refueling wing

Kaiser Aluminum's Trentwood rolling mill has been part of Spokane Valley since the federal government built it in 1942 to supply metal for wartime aircraft. In April 2026 The Spokesman-Review reported about 850 people working at the mill, which has concentrated on aerospace and airline markets since the mid-2000s and makes heat-treated aluminum sheet and plate that ends up in Boeing and Airbus aircraft, along with defense products. The company's chief executive told the paper that demand was as strong as he had ever seen it.

The City of Spokane Valley's aerospace page counts more than 8,000 people in airframe production across the region. It names suppliers such as AMI Metals, a cut-to-size service center for aerospace aluminum; Novation, which anodizes, plates, paints and tests parts in a 35,000-square-foot facility; and SkyOne Aerospace, which repairs and overhauls oil controls for the C-130, P-3 Orion and E-2 Hawkeye. Wagstaff, founded in 1946, designs and builds aluminum casting equipment in Spokane Valley, and when the AWS Spokane Section announced a tour of the plant in 2025 it described an extensive in-house welding program covering codes, processes, automation and quality control.

West of the city, Fairchild Air Force Base is home to the 92nd Air Refueling Wing and its KC-135 Stratotankers. Military construction and maintenance at a base of that size, from hangars to fuel systems, adds to the structural and piping work that contractors across the region bid on.

WABO, and why Washington welder examiners hold the CWI

Washington's building codes require structural welders to be qualified, and the Washington Association of Building Officials (WABO) runs a voluntary welder certification program that gives building officials, owners and engineers a uniform way to document that qualification. Its Standard 27-13, in the twelfth edition of June 2023, applies to welders, welding operators and tackers on structural steel, sheet steel, seismic and reinforcing steel work, and it reflects AWS D1.1, D1.3, D1.4 and the D1.8 seismic supplement.

The detail that matters to a CWI candidate is who gives those tests. To be approved as a WABO welder examiner, an applicant must submit proof of AWS CWI certification and qualification under AWS QC1, pass WABO's written welder examiner test, and renew the examiner card every year. A Spokane-area CWI can therefore go on to run WABO welder qualification tests for a testing agency, a college or a fabricator, a role that inspectors in most other states do not have in the same form. WABO also registers special inspection agencies and inspectors for building construction, and the Seattle CWI page explains that registration route.

Welders keep a WABO certification valid through endorsement by a supervisor, and anyone who goes more than six months without using the process has to test again. Someone has to run and witness all of those tests, and in Washington that person holds the CWI.

Bridges and highway steel on the North Spokane Corridor

The largest construction program in the city is the North Spokane Corridor, the new US 395 freeway that the Washington State Department of Transportation is building from the north side of Spokane toward Interstate 90. The Spokesman-Review reported in April 2026 that Kuney Construction, which has built more than 20 bridges on the corridor, had won the contract for the Mission-to-Alki segment, that the Spokane River crossing was expected to be finished that summer, and that the state had the corridor on track for completion in late 2030, with the Interstate 90 connection still to come.

Many of the corridor's structures use prestressed concrete girders, yet bridge work still involves welded steel: bearings, expansion joints, railings, sign structures and steel girders wherever the design calls for them. Steel bridge members for public owners are normally fabricated to AWS D1.5, the Bridge Welding Code, which has its own fracture-critical provisions and is stricter than D1.1 in several areas. A CWI who expects to work for a fabricator supplying bridge steel, or for an owner inspecting it, should consider D1.5 for Part C. Background reading: AWS D1.5.

Five questions that settle Part C for a Spokane candidate

Part C is an open-book test on one code, chosen when you apply. Work through these questions in order and stop at the first yes:

  1. Do you inspect building steel or plan to examine structural welders? AWS D1.1:2020 is the natural choice, and the WABO standard draws on it.
  2. Is most of your work on bridge or highway steel? AWS D1.5:2020 suits fabricators and inspectors on state and county bridge contracts.
  3. Do you weld or inspect aluminum structures and equipment? AWS D1.2:2014, the structural aluminum code, is on the AWS list and fits shops that build aluminum frames, platforms and machinery.
  4. Do your customers' drawings call for aerospace fusion welding? AWS D17.1:2024 covers it, but confirm that your work actually invokes it before choosing it.
  5. Is your work on pressure piping, boilers or plant systems? The ASME option, Section IX with B31.1 and B31.3, fits utility, food plant and process piping work.

Choose the book you will keep using after the exam, because Part C rewards knowing where things are rather than memorizing them. Useful reading: AWS D1.1 and WPS, PQR and WPQ explained.

Section 167, Big Bend and Spokane Community College

AWS lists the Spokane Section as Section 167 in District 19, alongside the Alaska, Greater Oregon, Puget Sound Olympic and Inland Empire sections and two Canadian sections. The Spokane Section opened its 2026-27 season with a kickoff meeting at Iron Workers Local 14 in September 2026, and its October meeting reviewed technology seen at FABTECH 2026. Its student chapter is at Big Bend Community College in Moses Lake. For a CWI candidate, section meetings are a practical way to meet inspectors who have sat the exam recently and to hear which code books local employers favor.

Spokane Community College teaches a three-quarter, competency-based Welding and Fabrication program covering shielded metal arc, oxy-acetylene, MIG and TIG welding, with blueprint reading, layout and shop equipment, in day and evening options. Students can move ahead when they finish competencies early. Graduates entering the trade should start an employment log from their first job, because welding education shortens the experience AWS requires, but only verifiable work counts toward the rest.

Planning the Part B trip from the Inland Northwest

Spokane candidates take Part A and Part C as computer-based tests at a Prometric site once AWS has accepted the application and issued an eligibility code. Part B is given only where AWS runs its CWI seminars, and the AWS list of CWI training locations in November 2026 had nothing in Washington, Oregon, Idaho or Montana. The listed sites nearest to Spokane were Sacramento and Los Angeles in California, Denver and Anchorage, so most candidates here should expect to fly for the practical. Look at the AWS seminar and exam schedule before you fix a study plan, and leave room for a retake in case one part falls short of the 72 percent AWS requires on each.

A trip that long is worth planning around. Book travel only after AWS confirms your eligibility, arrive the day before, and bring the identification and confirmation letter AWS asks for. The CWI exam budget calculator helps you add flights, lodging and unpaid days to the plan.

A study sequence for production and shift workers

Most Spokane candidates prepare while holding a full-time job, and many work rotating or overtime-heavy production shifts. The online format follows the same six-day outline, but you set the order and the pace. One sequence that works for people in that position:

  1. Foundations first. Welding processes, joint design, welding symbols and terminology, which underpin everything else and which production welders often know by hand but have never had to put into words.
  2. Metallurgy and heat. Preheat, heat input, cooling rate and how carbon steel, stainless steel and aluminum behave, the last being familiar ground in a valley built around aluminum.
  3. Testing and inspection methods. Destructive tests and the main NDT methods, including what each one can and cannot find, supported by the free NDT practice tests.
  4. Gauges and real welds. Measuring fillet size, convexity, undercut and misalignment on shop welds, plus visual inspection rehearsal in the Practical NDT welding workshop.
  5. The code book. Tab it, then answer timed questions until you can reach any acceptance table quickly.

Questions go to the instructor whenever they come up, so a topic that has you stuck at the end of a swing shift does not have to wait for a set time.

The six days inside a Spokane Valley plant

For a manufacturer or fabricator with several people heading for the exam, the corporate format brings the course to the plant. The practical day can use the company's own production welds and rejects, including aluminum where that is what the shop builds, together with its own gauges and its procedure and welder qualification records. The code day can be built on D1.1 for a structural shop, D1.2 for an aluminum fabricator or the ASME option for a plant engineering group. The weeks are the employer's call, so the course can sit between production peaks or around a planned shutdown.

Even inside a company group, the certification belongs to the individual. Every participant applies to AWS personally, provides their own vision test and experience evidence and sits each part of the exam in their own name, regardless of who pays.

The paperwork AWS asks of Spokane candidates

AWS counts years of welding-related work against education. A bachelor's degree in welding engineering or welding technology leaves one year to show. An associate or higher degree in welding, engineering technology, engineering or a physical science leaves two, engineering or technical courses that apply toward a welding bachelor's leave three, completed trade or vocational courses leave four, and a high school diploma or equivalent leaves five. With eighth-grade schooling the figure becomes nine years, and with less it is twelve. AWS judges what qualifies, and the work must be verifiable.

In Spokane's manufacturing economy many candidates have welded in production, maintenance and repair roles for several employers. For each one, record the dates, the processes and materials, the standard the work followed and any inspection-type duties, such as checking first articles, filling in weld logs or witnessing welder tests. A welder who has taken WABO tests should keep copies of those certifications, since they document process and position experience.

The vision requirement is met with the AWS visual acuity form, completed by an eye-care or medical professional, showing near vision of Jaeger J2 or equivalent at 12 inches or more, with correction if needed, and a color perception test. AWS limits how old that form can be on exam day, so book the test shortly before you apply. The CWI requirements guide covers the details.

After the CWI in the Inland Northwest

A new Spokane CWI might examine welders for WABO tests, inspect structural steel for a testing agency, or run welding quality in a manufacturing plant. Those who also want to carry out nondestructive testing need method training and certification by their employer under its written practice. Atlantis provides training based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A for that, for example VT Level 2, PT Level 2 for surface cracks in aluminum and stainless parts and UT Level 2, and the employer certifies the technician afterwards. The CWI is renewed at the third and sixth years of its nine-year cycle and recertified at the ninth through one of the AWS routes, which include retaking Part B or documenting 80 professional development hours; the Senior CWI pathway opens later in a career.

Local and nearby pages: NDT training in Spokane, ultrasonic testing in Spokane, magnetic particle testing in Spokane, NDT training in the Pacific Northwest and CWI exam prep in Portland.

Sending a Spokane enquiry

Tell us how many people the course is for, which format you prefer, which code book you expect to use for Part C and roughly when you plan to sit the exam. For a group at your site, include the plant location and the weeks that suit production. If you are not sure your experience will satisfy AWS, describe it briefly and we will point out what to confirm with AWS before you start. Fees are quoted on request. We reply within one business day.

faq.q: Is there an AWS section in Spokane?
faq.a: Yes. AWS lists the Spokane Section as Section 167 in District 19, with a student chapter at Big Bend Community College. Its 2026-27 season began with a kickoff meeting at Iron Workers Local 14 in September 2026.

faq.q: Why do WABO welder examiners need to be CWIs?
faq.a: WABO Standard 27-13 asks anyone applying to become a welder examiner for proof of AWS CWI certification and qualification under AWS QC1, a pass on WABO's written examiner test and an examiner card renewed every year. In Washington the CWI is therefore the starting point for running WABO structural welder tests.

faq.q: Where do Spokane candidates take Part B?
faq.a: At an AWS seminar location. The November 2026 AWS list had none in Washington, Oregon, Idaho or Montana, so plan a trip to a listed city such as Sacramento, Los Angeles, Denver or Anchorage. Parts A and C are computer-based tests at Prometric.

faq.q: Should someone from an aluminum shop choose AWS D1.2 for Part C?
faq.a: It can make sense if you inspect welded aluminum structures and equipment every day. If most of the welding around you is structural carbon steel, or you plan to examine WABO welder tests, AWS D1.1 is usually the better long-term choice.

faq.q: Does an aerospace supplier inspector in Spokane need D17.1?
faq.a: Only when the work invokes it. Many Inland Northwest aerospace suppliers machine, finish, distribute or overhaul parts rather than weld them, so check your customers' specifications before choosing D17.1:2024 over D1.1 or D1.2.

faq.q: Can a Spokane Valley manufacturer host the six days?
faq.a: Yes. The corporate format runs at the employer's site with its own production welds, gauges and qualification records, and the code day can follow the book the shop works to. Each participant applies to AWS individually.

faq.q: I completed the Spokane Community College welding program. Does that reduce the experience I need?
faq.a: Completed trade or vocational courses can bring the AWS requirement down from five years with a high school diploma to four, and qualifying degrees reduce it further. AWS decides how each program is classed, so include your course records with the application.

faq.q: Will my WABO welder certifications help the CWI application?
faq.a: They are useful evidence of the processes and positions you have welded, but AWS still needs verifiable years of welding-related work. File them with your employment records and supervisor contacts.

faq.q: How does Atlantis quote for Spokane candidates?
faq.a: Send the format, the number of people, your Part C code and the period when you want to test through the enquiry link on this page. Fees are quoted on request, and the reply arrives within one business day.
